title: What is Flink state management — keyed state (partitioned by key, exclusive per key: ValueState, ListState, MapState, ReducingState, AggregatingState) vs operator state (scoped to one parallel task: ListState, UnionListState, BroadcastState), and when do you use each?

s1_definition.profdef: Flink state is the data an operator remembers across events so it can compute results that depend on history, and it is managed and made fault-tolerant by Flink through checkpoints. There are two categories. Keyed state is partitioned by the stream's key and is accessible only within the context of the current key, so each key has its own independent slice of state, exposed through primitives like ValueState, ListState, MapState, ReducingState, and AggregatingState. Operator state is scoped to a single parallel operator instance rather than to a key, and is exposed through ListState, UnionListState, and BroadcastState, typically used by sources and sinks to remember things like offsets or broadcast rules.
s1_definition.analogy: Flink state is the memory of the bank's processing clerks. Keyed state is like giving each customer their own passbook: when a transaction for Rajesh arrives, the clerk opens only Rajesh's passbook, updates his running balance, and never touches Priya's passbook, because the state is strictly partitioned per customer. Operator state is like the clerk's own desk notebook that belongs to the clerk, not to any one customer, for example a note of "the last page number I read from the incoming ledger file," which the clerk needs to resume correctly after a break. Keyed state answers "what do I remember about this customer," while operator state answers "what does this worker itself need to remember."
s1_definition.oneliner: Keyed state is per-key memory accessed inside a keyed stream, while operator state is per-parallel-instance memory used by sources, sinks, and broadcasts.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flink state is the data an operator remembers across events so it can compute results that depend on history, and it is managed and made fault-tolerant by Flink through checkpoints. There are two categories. Keyed state is partitioned by the stream's key and is accessible only within the context of the current key, so each key has its own independent slice of state, exposed through primitives like ValueState, ListState, MapState, ReducingState, and AggregatingState. Operator state is scoped to a single parallel operator instance rather than to a key, and is exposed through ListState, UnionListState, and BroadcastState, typically used by sources and sinks to remember things like offsets or broadcast rules.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Flink state is the memory of the bank's processing clerks. Keyed state is like giving each customer their own passbook: when a transaction for Rajesh arrives, the clerk opens only Rajesh's passbook, updates his running balance, and never touches Priya's passbook, because the state is strictly partitioned per customer. Operator state is like the clerk's own desk notebook that belongs to the clerk, not to any one customer, for example a note of "the last page number I read from the incoming ledger file," which the clerk needs to resume correctly after a break. Keyed state answers "what do I remember about this customer," while operator state answers "what does this worker itself need to remember."

**One line to remember:** Keyed state is per-key memory accessed inside a keyed stream, while operator state is per-parallel-instance memory used by sources, sinks, and broadcasts.

sections.s2_technical:
Keyed state is only available on a keyed stream, that is after a `keyBy`. Flink automatically scopes the state to the current key, so your code simply reads and writes "the state," and Flink routes it to the right key's slice. `ValueState<T>` holds a single value per key, such as a running balance: `balance.update(balance.value().add(amount))`. `ListState<T>` holds a list per key, useful for buffering events. `MapState<K,V>` holds a map per key, useful for per-key sub-keyed lookups. `ReducingState<T>` keeps a single value that is incrementally combined by a reduce function as elements are added. `AggregatingState<IN,OUT>` is similar but lets the input and output types differ via an aggregate function. You declare keyed state by registering a `StateDescriptor` in the operator's `open` method and accessing it through `getRuntimeContext().getState(descriptor)`. Because keyed state is partitioned by key, Flink can rescale a job by redistributing key groups across the new parallelism, which is why keyed state scales cleanly.

Operator state is scoped to one parallel subtask and does not depend on a key. The common uses are in sources and sinks. `ListState` for operator state holds a list per subtask, and on rescaling Flink redistributes the list elements round-robin across the new subtasks, which is how a Kafka source splits its assigned partition offsets. `UnionListState` is a variant where, on restore, every subtask receives the union of all elements from all subtasks, which is needed when each instance must see the full set, such as a source that must re-divide all offsets itself. `BroadcastState` is a special map-based operator state used with a broadcast stream so that a small, slowly-changing dataset like a rules table is replicated identically to every parallel instance. You implement operator state through the `CheckpointedFunction` interface or `ListCheckpointed`, implementing `snapshotState` to write and `initializeState` to restore.

When do you use each? Use keyed state for anything that is naturally per-entity, which in a banking stream is almost everything: per-account balances, per-card fraud counters, per-customer session data. It is the default and the one you reach for most. Use operator state for the plumbing that is per-worker rather than per-entity: source read positions, sink buffers awaiting commit, and broadcast rule or configuration tables. The senior nuance is that keyed state is far more common and rescales gracefully by key group, while operator state requires you to think explicitly about how its contents redistribute when you change parallelism, and that broadcast state must be kept small because it is fully replicated to every instance. Both kinds are snapshotted into checkpoints so the job can recover with exactly-once consistency, and the choice of state backend determines whether that state lives on the JVM heap or in an embedded on-disk store.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants a real-time running balance per account that survives failures, so that each incoming transaction updates only that account's balance and the state is isolated from other accounts. Because this is naturally per-account, and each account's balance must be independent and must rescale cleanly as we add processing capacity, this is exactly keyed state, specifically a ValueState holding the running balance per account.

Problem 2 — The same job reads from a transaction log and must remember how far it has read in each input partition so that after a crash it resumes from the right position rather than reprocessing or skipping. This read position belongs to the worker reading the partition, not to any account, and must be redistributed correctly if we change parallelism. This is exactly operator state, specifically a ListState of read offsets owned by each source subtask.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that simulates both state kinds. We define a `Transaction` with an account id and amount. A `KeyedBalanceState` reproduces per-key ValueState by holding a map from account id to running balance and exposing update-under-key semantics, so updating Rajesh never touches Priya. A `SourceOffsetState` reproduces operator ListState by holding, per source subtask, the last read offset of each input partition, with a snapshot and restore method to mimic checkpointing. A `StateManagementDemo` main class streams transactions, updates the keyed balance per account, advances the source offsets, then simulates a crash and restore to show that both the per-account balances and the source offsets come back intact.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transactions, two for Rajesh (SAV2001) and two for Priya (CUR3001), all read from source partition zero at offsets 100 through 103, with keyed balance state and operator offset state.

Step 1: The first transaction credits Rajesh 1000. The keyed balance state opens Rajesh's slice, which starts at zero, and updates it to 1000. Priya's slice is untouched. The operator offset state records that partition zero has been read up to offset 100.

Step 2: The second transaction credits Priya 500. The keyed state opens Priya's independent slice and sets it to 500, while Rajesh's 1000 is untouched, demonstrating per-key isolation. The offset state advances partition zero to 101.

Step 3: The third transaction debits Rajesh 200. The keyed state opens Rajesh's slice, reads 1000, and updates to 800. The offset state advances to 102. Again Priya is unaffected.

Step 4: The fourth transaction credits Priya 300. Her slice goes from 500 to 800. The offset state advances to 103. Now Rajesh is at 800 and Priya is at 800, each tracked in its own keyed slice.

Step 5: A checkpoint is taken. Flink snapshots the keyed balance state, partitioned by key group, and the operator offset state for the subtask. The snapshot captures Rajesh 800, Priya 800, and partition zero offset 103.

Step 6: A crash is simulated by discarding the in-memory objects. On restore, the keyed state is rebuilt so Rajesh and Priya both return as 800, and the operator offset state is rebuilt so the source resumes reading partition zero from offset 103 rather than reprocessing from 100. Both state kinds survived, proving fault tolerance.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] KEYED ValueState[SAV2001] 0 -> 1000
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] KEYED ValueState[CUR3001] 0 -> 500
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] KEYED ValueState[SAV2001] 1000 -> 800
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] KEYED ValueState[CUR3001] 500 -> 800
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] CHECKPOINT taken. balances={SAV2001=800, CUR3001=800} offsets={0=103}
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] KEYED state restored: {SAV2001=800, CUR3001=800}
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] OPERATOR state restored subtask 0: {0=103}
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] After restore SAV2001 balance = 800
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] After restore CUR3001 balance = 800

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Memento Pattern: snapshot/restore capture+rebuild state       │
  │   WHY: checkpoint and recover without exposing internals      │
  │ Strategy Pattern: state backend (heap vs rocksdb) swappable   │
  │   WHY: same state API, different storage                      │

  │ L: any state object supports snapshot/restore                 │
  │ I: narrow update/value/snapshot/restore methods               │

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ KeyedBalanceState        │        │ SourceOffsetState         │
  │ (KEYED, per account)     │        │ (OPERATOR, per subtask)   │
  │──────────────────────────│        │──────────────────────────│
  │ - balanceByKey: Map      │        │ - subtaskId: int          │
  │──────────────────────────│        │ - offsets: Map<part,off>  │
  │ + update(acct, delta)    │        │──────────────────────────│
  │ + value(acct): BigDecimal│        │ + advance(part, offset)   │
  │ + snapshot(): Map        │        │ + snapshot(): Map         │
  │ + restore(Map)           │        │ + restore(Map)            │
  └──────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘
       per-key isolation                   per-subtask plumbing

  ── Keyed State Primitive Map ─────────────────────────────────

  ValueState<T>        single value per key      (balance)
  ListState<T>         list per key              (buffered events)
  MapState<K,V>        map per key               (sub-keyed lookups)
  ReducingState<T>     incrementally reduced     (running min/max)
  AggregatingState<I,O> aggregate, I != O        (running average)

  Operator State: ListState (round-robin on rescale),
                  UnionListState (full union on restore),
                  BroadcastState (replicated to all instances)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ────────────────────────────────

  1. balances.update("SAV2001", +1000) → keyed slice 0 → 1000
  2. offsets.advance(0, 100) → operator state partition 0 = 100
  3. ... process all txns
  4. CHECKPOINT: balances.snapshot(), offsets.snapshot()
  5. CRASH → new objects
  6. balancesAfter.restore(snap) → SAV=800, CUR=800
  7. offsetsAfter.restore(snap) → resume partition 0 at 103
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink state is the memory an operator keeps across events so it can compute results that depend on history, and Flink makes that state fault-tolerant by snapshotting it into checkpoints. There are two fundamentally different categories. Keyed state is partitioned by the stream's key and is only accessible after a keyBy, within the context of the current key, so every key gets its own completely independent slice of state and updating one key never touches another. Flink gives you several keyed primitives: ValueState for a single value per key such as a running balance, ListState for a list per key, MapState for a map per key, ReducingState for a value that is incrementally combined by a reduce function, and AggregatingState which is like ReducingState but allows the input and output types to differ. Because keyed state is partitioned by key, Flink can rescale a job by redistributing key groups across the new parallelism, which is why keyed state scales so cleanly.

Operator state is scoped to a single parallel operator instance rather than to a key, and it is the plumbing state that sources and sinks need. ListState for operator state holds a per-subtask list that Flink redistributes round-robin when you rescale, which is how a Kafka source splits its partition offsets. UnionListState is a variant where every subtask gets the full union of all elements on restore, needed when each instance must see everything. BroadcastState is a map-based operator state used with a broadcast stream to replicate a small, slowly-changing dataset like a rules table identically to every instance. You implement operator state through the CheckpointedFunction interface, writing in snapshotState and restoring in initializeState.

The rule for when to use each is straightforward. Keyed state is the default and by far the most common, because in a banking stream almost everything is naturally per-entity: per-account balances, per-card fraud counters, per-customer sessions. Operator state is for the per-worker plumbing: source read positions, sink buffers awaiting commit, and broadcast rule tables. At the National Bank of India our running-balance job used keyed ValueState for each account's balance so that a transaction only ever touched that account's slice and the job rescaled cleanly as we grew, and it used operator ListState in the source to remember how far each partition had been read so that after a crash it resumed from the exact offset instead of reprocessing or skipping. When I took a checkpoint, both the per-account balances and the source offsets were snapshotted to durable storage, and after a simulated crash both came back intact, which is exactly the exactly-once behavior regulators expect from a financial system. Being able to name the keyed primitives, contrast them with the operator-state variants, and explain which fits per-entity logic versus per-worker plumbing is what shows real command of Flink state.

Watermark: handle late data — discard after threshold
Checkpoint: fault tolerance — recover state on failure
